# Motivation and significance

Regularized generalized linear models (GLMs) — the L1, L2 and
elastic-net penalized fits provided by `glmnet` [@friedman2010glmnet;
@simon2011glmnetcox; @tay2023glmnetall] — are a workhorse of applied
statistics in R. `glmnet`'s numerical core is mature, but its user
interface is deliberately minimal: the caller supplies a
pre-constructed numeric design matrix `x` and a response `y`, and every
step that `stats::glm()` normally handles on the user's behalf —
formula parsing, factor encoding, contrast bookkeeping, complete-case
filtering, rank checking, and prediction-time design-matrix
reconstruction — is pushed to the caller. In practice this yields
three recurring hazards.

**Predict-time drift.** When the training design matrix is built by
`model.matrix(~ ., data = train)` and the test design matrix by
`model.matrix(~ ., data = test)` independently, a factor level that
appears only in `train` (or only in `test`) silently produces
different numbers of columns, and `predict.glmnet` fails with a
low-level "number of variables in newx must be N" error. In hosted
scoring pipelines this failure mode is common and hard to debug
because the mismatch is between two independently-constructed design
matrices rather than between the model and its input.

**Rank deficiency.** `stats::glm()` reports rank-deficient columns
with `NA` coefficients; `glmnet` accepts collinear columns silently.
A "zero" coefficient in a raw `glmnet` fit can therefore mean either
"shrunk to zero by the penalty" or "not identifiable in the design",
and the two are impossible to distinguish from the fit object alone.

**No inference contract.** Post-selection standard errors for
regularized fits are an unresolved statistical problem
[@tibshirani2016selective], yet callers routinely bolt classical
SE / z / p / CI onto `glmnet` coefficients using the raw penalized
Hessian. Existing wrappers give no explicit signal that these
quantities are unreliable.

`fbrglm` addresses all three by wrapping `glmnet` behind a
`glm()`-compatible formula interface that freezes the training-time
model recipe onto the fit object, restores `glm()`'s rank-deficient
NA convention, and prints an explicit inference policy in place of
untrustworthy classical statistics. The underlying `glmnet` and
`cv.glmnet` calls are unchanged. Interface / workflow packages are
an established category of scientific-software contribution — the
`tidyomics` ecosystem [@hutchison2024tidyomics], for example, was
recognized in *Nature Methods* not for introducing new estimators
but for imposing a unified interface across pre-existing tools.
`fbrglm` occupies the analogous role for `glmnet`.

# Software description

## Software architecture

The released package is installed from CRAN with
`install.packages("fbrglm")`; the development HEAD tracked in this
revision is available via
`remotes::install_github("dsc-chiba-u/fbrglm")`.

`fbrglm` exposes two user-facing entry points — `fbrglm()` for a fixed
grid of `lambda` values and its `lambda = "cv_min"` / `"cv_1se"`
shortcuts that delegate to `cv.glmnet` — and a family of `glm()`-style
S3 methods that operate on the returned `regularized_glm` object.

`fbrglm()` parses the formula against the training data, extracts the
`terms` object, `xlevels` (factor levels seen at fit time), and
`contrasts`, builds the numeric design matrix, and hands the pair
`(x, y)` to `glmnet::glmnet` (or `glmnet::cv.glmnet`) verbatim. It
then wraps the returned `glmnet` (or `cv.glmnet`) object together
with the frozen model recipe, a rank check performed by QR-pivot on
the column-centered design matrix (`qr_tol = 1e-7`, with
`rank_policy` selecting drop vs keep), and a small `nobs_info`
bookkeeping record (`n_total` / `n_dropped_missing` / `n_used`) into a
single `regularized_glm` object.

## Software functionalities

Table 2 lists the S3 methods that operate on a `regularized_glm`.
Each method has direct `glm()` semantics.

```{r methods-table, echo = FALSE}
methods_df <- data.frame(
  Method    = c("print", "summary", "coef", "predict", "nobs",
                "plot", "tidy", "glance",
                "as_glmnet", "as_cv_glmnet"),
  Purpose   = c(
    "compact display of family, lambda, and nobs_info",
    "coefficient table with NA for rank-deficient columns and an explicit inference-policy notice",
    "coefficient vector at the selected lambda; NA preserved for dropped columns",
    "reconstructs the design matrix from stored terms / xlevels / contrasts; supports on_new_levels = 'error' (default) or 'na'",
    "returns n_used from nobs_info",
    "diagnostic residual plots (default), or the underlying glmnet coefficient path / cv.glmnet curve",
    "broom-compatible tidy tibble of coefficients",
    "broom-compatible one-row model-level tibble",
    "accessor returning the underlying glmnet object",
    "accessor returning the underlying cv.glmnet object"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(methods_df, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE,
             caption = "S3 methods defined on the regularized\\_glm class.",
             linesep = "") |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position") |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(1, width = "2.5cm") |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(2, width = "10cm")
```

Supported model families are the full `glmnet` surface — `gaussian`,
`binomial`, `poisson`, `cox`, `multinomial`, `mgaussian` — plus
arbitrary `stats::family` objects such as `stats::Gamma` and
`MASS::negative.binomial` (with a fixed dispersion `theta`). Native
Cox is invoked with a `Surv()` response and `family = "cox"`; the
vignette also walks through the piecewise exponential Poisson
formulation as an alternative.

The prediction path reconstructs the design matrix against the
**stored** `terms` and `xlevels` — not against the levels present in
`newdata` — which is where most `glmnet` callers get injured. A
factor level unseen at fit time raises a clear error by default;
`on_new_levels = "na"` returns `NA` for the affected rows instead.

# Illustrative examples

## Binomial regression on `birthwt` with factor drift and rank deficiency

We use `MASS::birthwt` [@MASS], the canonical low-birth-weight cohort
(Springfield, MA, 1986; 189 obstetric records with `low`, an indicator
for birth weight below 2500 g, as the response). It exercises every
safety feature `fbrglm` adds on top of `glmnet`: an ethnicity factor
whose level definition is lost by common downstream cleaning, a
"cleaned" derived column that turns out to be a linear combination
of an existing factor (a classic data-engineering accident that
surfaces as rank deficiency), and the `glm()`-style coefficient /
summary contract on the fit object.

```{r birthwt-setup, include = FALSE}
## Silently run the same setup shown below so `fit` / `train` / `test`
## exist for the diagnostic-plot chunk.
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(fbrglm); library(MASS)})
data("birthwt", package = "MASS")
birthwt$race  <- factor(birthwt$race,  1:3, c("white","black","other"))
birthwt$smoke <- factor(birthwt$smoke, 0:1, c("no","yes"))
birthwt$ftv   <- factor(birthwt$ftv)
birthwt$any_visit <- as.integer(birthwt$ftv != "0")
set.seed(93); idx <- sample.int(nrow(birthwt), 150)
train <- birthwt[idx, ]; test <- birthwt[-idx, ]
suppressMessages({
  fit <- fbrglm(low ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ftv + any_visit,
                data = train, family = "binomial",
                lambda = "fix", lambda_value = 0.05)
})
```

```{r birthwt, eval = FALSE}
library("fbrglm")
library("MASS")

data("birthwt", package = "MASS")
birthwt$race  <- factor(birthwt$race,  1:3, c("white", "black", "other"))
birthwt$smoke <- factor(birthwt$smoke, 0:1, c("no",    "yes"))
birthwt$ftv   <- factor(birthwt$ftv)

## Data-engineering accident: a downstream ETL job added a "cleaned"
## indicator for any prenatal visit. `any_visit` is a linear function
## of the `ftv` dummies + intercept, so the design matrix is
## rank-deficient once both live in the formula.
birthwt$any_visit <- as.integer(birthwt$ftv != "0")

set.seed(93)
idx   <- sample.int(nrow(birthwt), 150)
train <- birthwt[idx, ]
test  <- birthwt[-idx, ]

fit <- fbrglm(
    low ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ftv + any_visit,
    data         = train,
    family       = "binomial",
    lambda       = "fix",
    lambda_value = 0.05
)
#> fbrglm: dropped 1 linearly dependent column(s) (rank 11 / 12):
#>         any_visit. Their coefficients will be reported as NA,
#>         as in stats::glm().

summary(fit)
#> Observations: total = 150, dropped (missing) = 0, used = 150
#>
#> Coefficients: (1 not defined because of singularities: any_visit)
#>                Estimate
#>   (Intercept)   -0.3423
#>   age           -0.0027
#>   lwt           -0.0042
#>   raceblack      0.0000
#>   raceother      0.0000
#>   smokeyes       0.5156
#>   ptl            0.2526
#>   ftv1..ftv6     0.0000     (all shrunk to zero at this lambda)
#>   any_visit           NA
#>
#> Non-zero predictors (4): age, lwt, smokeyes, ptl
#> Note: no standard errors / z / p under infer = "none".
```

Two things to notice. First, `any_visit` shows `NA` in the coefficient
table — `fbrglm` detected the rank deficiency at fit time (QR-pivot
on the column-centered design matrix) and preserved `glm()`'s
convention, so a numeric zero elsewhere in the table unambiguously
means "shrunk by the penalty" rather than "not identifiable". Second,
`summary()` prints only point estimates and an inference-policy notice
in place of SE / z / p / CI; the classical Wald quantities are not
valid post-penalization [@tibshirani2016selective] and the package
refuses to display them by default.

The same `glm()`-shaped API extends to visual diagnostics. Calling
`plot(fit)` returns the three-panel deviance-residual view familiar
from `stats::glm` (Figure 1); raw `glmnet` does not expose
residuals in the `glm()` sense, so this view is a genuine `fbrglm`
add-on rather than a pass-through.

```{r birthwt-diag, echo = TRUE, fig.width = 7.2, fig.height = 1.7, out.width = "100%", fig.pos = "!h", fig.cap = "Standard \\texttt{glm}-style diagnostic panel produced by \\texttt{plot(fit)} on the \\texttt{birthwt} fit. Deviance residuals are computed from the family's \\texttt{dev.resids} at the selected \\texttt{lambda}; the two-arc shape is the binomial GLM signature. The panels are intended as an exploratory diagnostic: for binomial fits with small event counts, deviance residuals are not expected to be exactly normal, and they do not correct for penalty-induced shrinkage, so a formal assessment should rely on calibration curves and discrimination measures (c-statistic) rather than on the Q--Q panel alone."}
op <- graphics::par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(3.5, 3.5, 2, 0.5), mgp = c(2, 0.7, 0))
plot(fit)
graphics::par(op)
```

The split also stresses the predict path. R preserves factor levels
under ordinary subsetting, so the 0-`black` test slice above does
not by itself cause a column mismatch; that happens when a
downstream step (e.g. `droplevels`) erases the training-time level
definition and a hand-built `glmnet` call then raises "number of
variables in newx must be N". `predict(fit, newdata = ...)` on an
`fbrglm` fit succeeds, because the design matrix is reconstructed
against the **stored** `xlevels` rather than the levels present in
the newdata; a truly unseen level would raise a checked error by
default, or return `NA` under `on_new_levels = "na"`.

## Cox regression on `lung` with missing-data reporting

The same call pattern works for native Cox regression. Using
`survival::lung` [@survival2000], several covariates carry natural
missingness that `fbrglm`'s complete-case bookkeeping reports without
having to reason about it externally:

```{r lung-cox, eval = FALSE}
library("survival")
data("lung", package = "survival")
lung$ph.ecog <- factor(lung$ph.ecog)

cox_fit <- fbrglm(
    Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog + meal.cal + wt.loss,
    data         = lung,
    family       = "cox",
    lambda       = "fix",
    lambda_value = 0.02
)
#> fbrglm: dropped 58 row(s) with missing values (170 / 228 kept).

cox_fit$nobs_info
#> n_total = 228 ;  n_dropped_missing = 58 ;  n_used = 170
```

Any row with an `NA` in the response or in one of the predictors is
dropped, and the exact tally lands on the fit object — the same
`nobs_info` bookkeeping is available across every supported family.
The `vignette("fbrglm-families")` bundled with the package walks the
remaining families end-to-end using the same formula-first pattern.

# Impact

## Improvement to existing regularized-GLM analyses

`fbrglm` is directly applicable to any project that uses `glmnet` for
regularized GLMs — from small ad-hoc analyses to production scoring
pipelines. Four categories of failure that are common in raw-`glmnet`
code disappear at the API level:

- **Predict-time robustness.** Factor-level mismatch becomes a
  checked error — or controlled `NA` under `on_new_levels = "na"` —
  rather than a low-level `glmnet` crash. In the companion
  benchmark [@fbrglm-experiments], 3 of 5 tested workflows fail on a
  narrowed test factor; `fbrglm` and the hardhat-backed `parsnip`
  workflow are the two survivors.
- **Interpretability of "zero".** Rank-deficient columns show as
  `NA` coefficients (`glm()` convention), so a numeric zero means
  "shrunk by the penalty" rather than "not identifiable".
- **Inference contract.** The regularization contract is surfaced in
  every `summary()` call, pointing users to post-selection inference
  [@tibshirani2016selective] rather than to classical Wald statistics.
- **Interoperability.** `broom` [@broom] methods (`tidy`, `glance`)
  are provided directly, and two accessors return the underlying
  `glmnet` / `cv.glmnet` objects unchanged.

## Research workflows enabled

The safety layer changes what regularized GLMs can be trusted with,
not what they compute. Two workflow patterns that were previously
labor-intensive become routine: **hand-off between exploration and
production scoring**, where a serialized fit is applied to arriving
batches without re-materializing the training design matrix; and
**family-wide analyses**, where a study comparing, e.g., binomial,
negative binomial, and Gamma fits on the same cohort no longer needs
a family-specific wrapper per fit — the eight supported families all
share the `regularized_glm` return type. The companion benchmark
[@fbrglm-experiments] uses this uniformity for an
$8 \times 5 = 40$-cell parity sweep against raw `glmnet`,
`glmnetUtils` [@glmnetUtils], and a `parsnip` [@parsnip] /
`workflows` [@workflows] pipeline on rank-full designs; every
`fbrglm` cell matches raw `glmnet` to zero absolute difference.

## Changes in daily practice

For a working analyst, the diff against a raw-`glmnet` script is
concentrated in what used to be pure bookkeeping: `model.matrix()`
calls, their re-materialization at predict time, manual `xlevels`
maintenance, and per-family dispatch. All of these move into the
package, leaving the analysis script to say `formula + data + family`
and read back a `regularized_glm` object that behaves like a `glm`
fit for `print`, `summary`, `coef`, `predict`, `nobs`, `plot`, and
`broom` [@broom]. For tidymodels teams, the two `glmnet` accessors
keep `fbrglm` drop-in with existing downstream tooling.

## Adoption and reproducibility

`fbrglm` v0.0.1 was released to CRAN on 2026-07-09 and updated to
v0.1.0 on 2026-07-14. Continuous integration on GitHub runs `R CMD
check` on four platforms per push, and a companion Docker image on
Docker Hub and GHCR pins the exact R and package versions used in
this paper. In a small binomial runtime grid (5 iterations per
method/scenario, median reported; raw per-iteration timings in
`results/raw/runtime_small_raw.csv`) `fbrglm` sits within roughly
2–3$\times$ the raw-`glmnet` cost — comparable to `glmnetUtils` and
lighter than the `parsnip` / `workflows` path. The release is
archived at [@fbrglm] and the replication material at
[@fbrglm-experiments]; the MIT license permits academic and
commercial use.

**Inference and limitations.** Classical SE / z / p / CI are
suppressed because the penalized Hessian does not deliver valid Wald
quantities [@tibshirani2016selective]; valid routes are
sample-splitting with inference on the held-out half and selective
inference conditioning on the selection event
[@lee2016selective; @chatterjee2011bootstrap], available via
`selectiveInference` / `hdi`. `qr_tol` is user-configurable with
`stats::glm.fit`'s default [@golub2013matrix]; Cox, multinomial, and
mgaussian are experimental for unusual configurations; negative
binomial inherits `MASS::glm.nb`'s fixed-`theta` fit.

# Conclusions

`fbrglm` narrows the gap between `stats::glm()`'s strict
modeling-workflow contract and the numerical machinery of `glmnet`.
By freezing the training-time model recipe on the fit object,
restoring `glm()`'s rank-deficient NA convention, and printing an
explicit inference policy, the package removes a well-known class of
correctness and reproducibility failures that raw `glmnet` invites
but does not itself catch. The underlying estimator is unchanged;
what the user gets is the safety guarantees, error semantics, and
`glm()`-shaped API that make regularized GLMs safe to hand to a
production scoring pipeline.
